title: AI in Education #9: Five Things I Learned from Grainne Hallahan
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton summarizes five findings from Teacher Tapp's Grainne Hallahan, who aggregates daily survey data from over 10,000 UK teachers. Fifty-eight percent of secondary teachers caught a student using AI to cheat in the past month, but Hallahan believes the real rate is higher, since students are deliberately engineering different wrong answers across a class to avoid a suspicious pattern of perfect scores. Four in ten teachers have never taught students about AI and don't plan to, a stance Barton and Hallahan suggest may be a reasonable judgment given how poor free AI tools are for precision subjects. Teacher use of AI for lesson planning has grown to 20%, concentrated among the least experienced teachers, who are also least able to catch the errors AI introduces into unfamiliar subject matter. Roughly half of secondary teachers report their school has no AI policy, or don't know whether one exists even when senior leaders say it does. The standout finding closes the piece: teachers who believe they have improved as teachers are dramatically more likely to want to return after the summer (47% versus 29%), and Hallahan argues no AI tool can deliver that sense of growth — only a human mentor who notices and names it can.
points: Students are systematically engineering different wrong answers across a class to defeat AI-cheating detection, which suggests sanctioning cheating may simply incentivize more sophisticated concealment rather than reduce it.

Four in ten teachers choosing not to teach AI may be a reasonable professional judgment: free tools perform poorly on precision subjects, and novice learners who can't evaluate AI output may be worse off using it than not.

Novice teachers using AI to plan lessons in subjects they don't know deeply are in a riskier position than those using static trusted resources, because they lack the subject knowledge to catch the AI's errors before they reach students.

The school AI-policy gap — senior leaders believe a policy exists, but roughly half of secondary teachers don't know it does — is a governance failure with real accountability consequences, since a policy nobody has read cannot be enforced.

The strongest predictor of whether a teacher wants to return after summer is not pay or workload but whether they believe they have become a better teacher — a sense of growth that Hallahan argues comes from a human mentor, not from any AI tool.
quotes: We can debate the promise and peril of AI in education until we are blue in the face, but at some point, we have to ask: What are teachers actually doing? What are students actually doing? And does any of this match what the researchers and the builders think is happening?

They would screenshot their online homework, send it to ChatGPT, and get the answers. But they knew that if they all suddenly started getting 10 out of 10, the teacher would be suspicious. So they planned it out in advance: one would get question 3 wrong, another would get question 7 wrong. Different mistakes, different scores, no detectable pattern.

Of the teachers who did catch students cheating, 77% just spoke to the student, 35% asked them to redo the work, and only 13% issued a sanction. The sanction, assuming it's sufficiently unappealing to the student, is likely to provide the most significant incentive... but perhaps not the one we hope for.

The only reason I can use AI productively is because I have enough subject knowledge to evaluate the output, catch the errors, and push back when it is wrong. A Year 7 student who does not know whether 4.2 x 19 is closer to 80 or 800 - to borrow Barbara Oakley's example from earlier in this series - is in no position to catch a chatbot's mistake.

In secondary schools, 51% of teachers said their school has no AI policy for staff. But when Teacher Tapp asked senior leaders the same question, the vast majority said: “Of course we have an AI policy!

Gráinne’s point is simple: you cannot hold a teacher accountable for something you have not told them. If a parent complains that their child’s report was generated by AI, and you have no policy that says teachers should not be doing that, you have no leg to stand on.
Teachers who believed they had improved: 47% were looking forward to returning. Teachers who felt the same or worse: 29%. That was the only variable that produced the pattern.
No AI tool can do this. No policy can mandate it. It is a human relationship, built on observation and trust, delivered in a corridor or over a cup of tea.
